paper_title: History Forcing: Distilling History-Dependent Continuations for Long-Horizon Video World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient generation, yet maintaining consistency over long rollouts remains challenging, especially when subjects or scenes reappear after going out of sight. Despite progress in fidelity and rollout robustness, existing distillation methods do not fully exploit richer historical information to constrain the student's current prediction. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{History Forcing}, a unified on-policy distillation framework that strengthens historical supervision for few-step autoregressive video generators. The framework uses the residual between teacher predictions with and without informative historical context to decouple this supervision. Such a historical context can be obtained using earlier generated chunks with less accumulated drift or a fixed-view teacher rollout that keeps the scene visible while the student looks away. The residual is then weighted and added to the score or velocity prediction used for distillation, forming a corrected target. By aligning the student with this corrected target through distillation, History Forcing incorporates long-range historical constraints into autoregressive generation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among 1.3B models, with a VBench quality score of 85.07 for 15s video generation and a VBench-Long aggregate score of 79.82 for 60s generation. For out-of-sight world modeling, evaluations further demonstrate more plausible scene evolution and more consistent states when the camera returns, with Evolution Quality improving from 2.35 to 2.70 on PlayWorld and Object Consistency from 58.43 to 62.18 on MemoBench.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Few-step autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models have enabled efficient long-horizon video generation [39, 57, 63]. However, maintaining consistency over extended autoregressive rollouts remains challenging. Coherent continuation often relies on earlier observations of persistent subjects, scenes, and dynamics, yet such information may be insufficiently incorporated into later predictions, leading to gradual subject and scene drift. This reliance on long-range history becomes even more pronounced in video world models. When an entity leaves the field of view, it may reappear only after long interval, by which point the recent frames carry no information about it [16, 54]. These challenges make effective use of long-range history critical for consistent autoregressive generation. Existing training paradigms have progressively increased the role of historical information in autoregressive supervision. Teacher forcing conditions predictions on ground-truth prefixes [18, 31], whereas Self Forcing applies distribution matching distillation (DMD) to student-generated rollouts using bidirectional diffusion teacher [28]. Subsequent methods further improve long-horizon training by extending supervision to longer generated sequences, preserving information from earlier frames, or propagating learning signals from later predictions to earlier generated representations [39, 57, 73]. More recent approaches condition teacher predictions on longer contexts, causally matched prefixes, or privileged observations, allowing the distillation target to better reflect historical dependencies relevant to autoregressive generation [4, 11, 38]. Despite these advances, existing distillation targets do not provide an explicit mechanism to strengthen historical constraints independently of the teachers overall generative supervision. As illustrated in Fig. 2, DMD with bidirectional diffusion teacher provides strong supervision for video quality, but does not explicitly incorporate distant autoregressive history into teacher predictions. History-conditioned methods instead distill from an AR teacher with access to richer historical context [4, 11]. However, matching its full conditional distribution couples supervision for temporal consistency and visual quality. The AR teachers weaknesses in visual quality may therefore constrain the student [63]. We refer to this limitation as historyquality coupling. To address this limitation, we introduce History Forcing, unified on-policy distillation framework that isolates and strengthens historical supervision. We compare teacher predictions with and without informative historical context to compute residual that captures the influence of history on the current prediction. This residual is then weighted and added to the score or velocity prediction used for distillation, guiding the student to generate continuations consistent with the historical observations. We apply History Forcing to different tasks and develop corresponding history construction strategies. In long-video generation, we use earlier chunks of the students rollout to provide subject and scene information less affected by accumulated drift. The resulting residual corrects the DMD target while retaining the bidirectional teachers supervision for visual quality. For out-of-sight world modeling, we obtain history from teacher rollout that keeps the camera fixed on the region to model its evolution while the region is outside the students view. This history is used to compute the residual that guides the students continuation upon revisit. As illustrated in Fig. 1, History Forcing better preserves subject appearance and scene structure over long rollouts and produces more consistent scene states upon revisit, demonstrating the benefits of strengthening historical supervision. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce History Forcing, unified distillation framework that decouples historical supervision 2 from generative supervision. By comparing teacher predictions with and without informative history, we compute context residual that is weighted and added to the original distillation target, allowing historical constraints to be strengthened independently. This formulation can be readily incorporated into DMD and on-policy self-distillation and is compatible with existing long-video training strategies. We develop history construction strategies for long-video generation and out-of-sight world modeling, using earlier generated chunks to constrain temporal drift and fixed-camera teacher rollouts to supervise scene evolution. History Forcing achieves VBench quality score of 85.07 for 15s generation and directly extrapolates to 60s generation with VBench-Long aggregate score of 79.82, using student training rollouts of at most 15s. With only 1.3B teachers, it outperforms the compared 1.3B models, including those distilled from 14B teachers, and approaches the 5B LongLive-2.0 model on VBench-Long. For out-of-sight world modeling, it further improves scene evolution and revisit consistency on PlayWorld and MemoBench.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Long-horizon autoregressive video diffusion. Existing video diffusion models provide strong visual and motion priors for short video synthesis [23, 33, 50, 58], while extending generation to long temporal horizons requires mitigating error accumulation and maintaining useful historical context. Training-free approaches extend pretrained models through diagonal denoising, temporal feature manipulation, and cache compression [32, 40, 60]. Autoregressive approaches instead improve the rollout process through extended self-rollouts, bounded contexts, rolling denoising, or error-aware training [8, 13, 20, 22, 25, 36, 39, 57, 59]. Context packing, learned memory representations, and history-aware supervision further improve access to earlier observations [5, 15, 43, 55, 6567, 73]. History-Guided Video Diffusion combines predictions under different historical conditions during sampling [45]. We instead design distillation targets that explicitly incorporate historical supervision into on-policy training. Few-step causal video diffusion distillation. Few-step causal video diffusion builds on diffusion and flow distillation to reduce autoregressive denoising costs [7, 10, 17, 21, 41, 42]. DMD and DMD2 establish distribution matching as an effective objective for few-step generation [61, 62]. CausVid uses DMD to distill few-step AR generator from bidirectional diffusion teacher, while Self Forcing further performs distillation on student-generated rollouts to reduce exposure bias [28, 63]. Subsequent work improves causal initialization and teacherstudent alignment [69, 70]: Causal Forcing uses an AR teacher for ODE initialization, while Context-Matched Distillation aligns teacher scoring with the causal context available to the student [4, 72]. Context Forcing incorporates longer history into an AR teachers conditional distribution, while OPSD-V uses real-video history to provide EMA velocity targets along student trajectories [11, 38]. These approaches improve sampling efficiency and teacherstudent alignment, but the contribution of historical context remains implicit in the target. History mechanisms in video world models. Historical conditioning is also central to video world models [52], where camera motion can separate revisit from its last informative observation. Video generation provides basis for interactive world simulation [2, 3, 6, 24, 34, 49, 71]. Real-time interactive systems combine controllable autoregressive generation with long-rollout training and scene memory [19, 48, 68]. WorldMem combines spatial and temporal cues for historical conditioning, while VMem uses geometry-indexed view retrieval to maintain cross-view consistency [35, 53, 64]. Memory Forcing trains models to balance temporal and spatial memory during exploration and revisits, while WorldPlay reconstitutes historical context and aligns teacher and student memory during distillation [27, 47]. LiveWorld uses historical references and fixed-view virtual monitors to preserve scene identity and continue unseen events, while ReMind trains models to recall reliable historical observations across occlusions and viewpoint changes [16, 54]. These methods improve scene consistency through memory mechanisms and history-aware training, but coherent continuation across long observation gaps remains challenging.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: History Forcing derives history-dependent correction by comparing AR teacher predictions for the same noisy student sample under two contexts that differ only in additional history. As shown in Fig. 3, this correction is applied to the reference score in DMD for long-horizon consistency and to the teacher velocity target in on-policy self-distillation for out-of-sight evolution. 4 Figure 4 Comparison of distillation targets, where + and denote distributions with and without additional history. (a) DMD uses reference close to the data distribution without history. (b) AR Distillation uses the history-conditioned AR distribution, with larger modeling error. (c) History Forcing transfers the history-induced shift from the AR teacher to the reference, producing target closer to the data distribution with history.

4.2 Distillation for Long-Horizon Consistency
To improve long-horizon consistency, we use the history-reweighted distribution in Eq. (6) as the target
for DMD. A pretrained bidirectional diffusion model defines the reference distribution, while a frozen AR
teacher provides the history-dependent correction.
sections.content: During long autoregressive rollouts, subject appearance and scene structure may gradually drift as generation errors accumulate. Earlier chunks can provide subject and scene information that is less affected by accumulated drift. To incorporate this information into distillation, we construct the additional 5 history hi from consecutive latent frames immediately preceding the shared recent context in the same student rollout. One AR teacher context combines this additional history with the recent latent frames in chronological order, whereas the other retains only the recent frames. Sharing the recent context helps preserve autoregressive continuity and avoid an excessive gap between the two conditional distributions. The residual between the two teacher scores provides history-dependent correction to the bidirectional reference score. As illustrated in Fig. 4, the reference distribution closely approximates the data distribution but does not incorporate the additional history. Direct AR distillation uses the history-conditioned AR distribution as the full target, tying historical supervision to the AR teachers generative accuracy. History Forcing instead retains the bidirectional reference score sref for visual-quality supervision and uses the posterior-gradient term in Eq. (7) to encourage consistency with the additional history, thereby decoupling historical supervision from matching the full AR distribution. sections.title:
4.3 Refinement for Out-of-Sight Evolution
In camera-controlled video world models, scene evolution during out-of-sight intervals poses an additional
challenge to long-horizon consistency. Earlier chunks of the student’s rollout provide historical observations
that constrain subject appearance and scene structure upon revisit, but do not capture changes occurring
outside the field of view. Historical supervision derived from these observations therefore provides limited
guidance for out-of-sight evolution.
sections.content: To provide supervision for out-of-sight evolution, we use teacher model to generate video from the same initial scene image as the student. The student follows its prescribed camera trajectory, whereas the teacher keeps the camera at its initial pose to model how the scene evolves while outside the students view. As illustrated in Fig. 3, we construct hi for each supervised student chunk using latent frames from the teachers fixed-camera rollout at timestamps preceding the start of that chunk. To extract supervision from this history, we compare teacher predictions with and without hi. The teachers inputs share the latent frames immediately preceding the current chunk in the students rollout to preserve continuity along the students camera trajectory. We refine the pretrained world model through on-policy self-distillation to improve out-of-sight evolution while preserving its visual quality. Because distilled few-step generator is not trained to provide accurate denoising predictions across arbitrary noise levels, directly using it as score teacher can be unreliable. Following OPSD-V [38], we instead supervise the students velocity predictions along its sampling trajectory using history-guided targets constructed from an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher. This formulation requires no auxiliary fake-score model. Let v+ EMA and EMA denote the teachers velocity predictions with and without hi, using the same noisy student chunk, timestep, prompt, and camera controls. sections.title:
5.1 Experimental Setup
Long-video generation. We initialize the bidirectional DMD teacher and the trainable fake-score model
from pretrained Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [50] weights. The AR student is initialized from the released causal ODE
checkpoint of Causal Forcing [72]. The AR teacher is initialized from Causal Forcing’s released multi-step
AR diffusion checkpoint, which was trained on 5s video clips. To assess the gains in student performance
from improving the AR teacher’s ability to model long-range dependencies, we further fine-tune this teacher
on 10s clips from UltraVideo-Long [56]. We train the student for 300 iterations on filtered and expanded
VidProM [51] prompts.
sections.content: Student training follows the long-rollout training strategy of Self-Forcing++ [13]. Rollout durations are uniformly sampled between 5s and 15s, with DMD supervision applied to the final 5s window. Both AR teacher inputs share the latest 6 student-generated latent frames. The history-conditioned input additionally includes the 12 latent frames immediately preceding this shared context. For efficiency, history supervision is restricted to 1 randomly sampled eligible chunk. Unless otherwise stated, historical supervision is applied with λ = 1 at diffusion timesteps < 750. Our baseline follows the Self-Forcing++ training strategy, using the same student initialization and training setup as History Forcing but without historical supervision. We evaluate 15s generation using VBench [29]. Following LongLive-2.0 [12], we use VBench-Long [30] to evaluate 60s videos generated from MovieGenBench prompts [44]. See Section A.1 for details. Out-of-sight world modeling. We initialize the world model from the released DreamX-World-5B [48] checkpoint, which also serves as the baseline. The training set contains 200 initial scene images from Pexels [1], each used with 4 camera trajectories that leave and return to the initial viewpoint, yielding 800 training samples. Our adapted OPSD-V [38] baseline uses fixed-view teacher rollouts in place of real-video teacher history and corresponds to the λ = 1 case of History Forcing. We fine-tune the model for 100 steps using LoRA, with supervision at all 4 denoising steps of the revisit chunks. Historical supervision strength. The timestep threshold τ restricts historical supervision to < τ , while λ controls its contribution to the DMD target. Table 4 varies each factor separately, keeping the other at its default value of τ = 750 or λ = 1. Reducing τ from 1000 to 500 raises the quality score from 84.62 to 85.08, whereas τ = 750 achieves the highest subject consistency (92.58). These results favor concentrating historical supervision at lower noise levels. In the weight ablation, increasing λ from 0.5 to 2 improves subject and background consistency but reduces dynamic degree. The highest quality score is achieved at λ = 1, indicating that moderate history weight balances historical constraints with the bidirectional teachers supervision for visual quality. In world-model self-distillation, Table 6 studies the number of supervised denoising steps and the history weight. With λ = 2 fixed, supervising all 4 steps yields better overall results across both benchmarks than supervising only the last 3 or 2 steps, supporting historical supervision throughout denoising. At λ = 1, the distillation target is the teachers velocity prediction conditioned on additional history. For out-of-sight revisits, recent student observations provide little information about the revisited region, making this history essential for constraining its identity and evolving state. Using λ > 1 amplifies the history-induced prediction change, placing greater emphasis on these constraints during self-distillation. The history-weight ablation favors λ = 3 across both benchmarks, indicating that stronger historical supervision benefits scene consistency and evolution across viewpoint changes. History construction. Table 5 studies the roles of shared recent context and initial sink frames. In the default setting, both AR teacher inputs share the latest 6 student-generated latent frames, while the + input additionally includes the 12 latent frames immediately preceding this shared context. Removing the 6 recent frames from the input reduces the quality score from 84.82 to 81.91 and lowers both consistency measures. Sharing recent context keeps the immediate history fixed, allowing the residual to capture the contribution of earlier observations. At the same history budget, replacing the oldest 3 frames in the + input with initial sink frames also lowers the quality score to 83.81 and reduces subject and background consistency. These results favor retaining consecutive earlier chunks for historical supervision, together with shared recent context that preserves autoregressive continuity. Gradient normalization. Table 7 examines whether the history term is jointly normalized with the DMD gradient. Standard DMD divides its distillation gradient by the mean absolute difference between the student-generated sample and the bidirectional teachers denoising prediction. Without joint normalization, the history term is added after this division. Joint normalization instead computes the normalization factor using the denoising target that includes the history term, then divides the combined DMD and history update by this factor. This increases the quality score from 84.09 to 84.82 and dynamic degree from 59.72 to 78.06, while the alternative yields higher subject and background consistency. These results favor joint normalization for balancing temporal consistency with motion dynamics. 9 Figure 5 Qualitative comparisons of consistency. (a) Temporal consistency in 60s autoregressive video generation with Self-Forcing, LongLive, Rolling Forcing, and History Forcing. (b,c) Revisit consistency in video world models, with each pair showing the baseline and History Forcing. Training efficiency. Table 8 reports the training overhead relative to DMD. By restricting historical supervision to one sampled chunk, we keep the increases in training time per step and peak allocated memory to only 2.31% and 1.99%, respectively. History Forcing thus achieves its quality and consistency gains with modest additional training cost.

sections.title:
5.4 Qualitative Comparison
Fig. 5 presents qualitative comparisons of temporal consistency in long-video generation and revisit
consistency in out-of-sight world modeling. In the 60s yoga example (a), Self-Forcing develops pronounced
color artifacts as generation progresses. LongLive exhibits limb duplication, while Rolling Forcing shows
leg deformations during pose transitions. History Forcing maintains more consistent body structure and
clothing appearance while preserving the park setting throughout the rollout. For camera-controlled revisits
(b,c), the baseline alters the drinking glass geometry and the colored-band layout. In contrast, History
Forcing retains the original glass shape and preserves the surrounding pattern as paint covers the pink
region. Additional qualitative examples are provided in Section B.
6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented History Forcing, which decouples historical supervision for few-step autoregressive video generators by comparing teacher predictions with and without informative history. The method augments DMD with long-range historical constraints while retaining the bidirectional teachers supervision for visual quality. Fixed-view teacher history further guides out-of-sight evolution through the OPSD velocity target. Experiments show that History Forcing reduces appearance and layout drift in long videos and better preserves object-state changes across out-of-sight intervals, producing more consistent states when the camera returns. Limitations and Future Work. Our experiments are limited to 1.3B teachers and students for long-video generation and 5B backbone for world modeling. Across both settings, historical supervision remains constrained by the underlying models ability to capture temporal dynamics. In world modeling, for example, limited scene evolution in fixed-view teacher rollouts can weaken supervision for out-of-sight state changes. Future work will explore larger teachers and students, longer-context training, and improvements to the world models ability to simulate physically plausible dynamics.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: In the Appendix, we provide the following: additional training, inference, and evaluation details in Appendix A. additional qualitative comparisons and examples of long-video generation and out-of-sight world modeling in Appendix B.

sections.title: A Additional Implementation Details
sections.content: Both applications use AdamW with betas (0, 0.999), weight decay 0.01, and maximum gradient norm of 10. Training uses 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 1 sample per GPU and random seed 42. Student sampling uses 4 SDE steps with unshifted timesteps (1000, 750, 500, 250) and timestep shift of 5. Each autoregressive chunk contains 3 latent frames, and videos are generated at 16 FPS. All context lengths below are measured in latent frames. A.1 Long-Video Generation Training. The student learning rate is 2 106, and the fake-score model learning rate is 4 107. The bidirectional and AR teachers remain frozen during student distillation. The bidirectional teacher uses classifier-free guidance scale of 3.0. The fake-score model is updated at every iteration and the student once every 5 iterations. Gradient accumulation over 8 steps gives an effective batch size of 64. The student EMA uses decay of 0.99 and is initialized at iteration 200. The chunk for historical supervision is sampled from the DMD supervision window. AR teacher fine-tuning uses teacher forcing with learning rate of 2 106 and an effective batch size of 8. For the 10s AR teacher, we use the fine-tuning checkpoint at iteration 2500. The AR teachers are configured with attention windows of 21 and 42 latent frames for the 5s and 10s variants, respectively. The two predictions use separate KV caches, with matched temporal positions for the current chunk. The threshold is applied to the shifted DMD scoring timestep. Joint normalization is used by default. Inference. KV window with 3 sink frames in both training and inference. Inference uses student EMA weights at 832 480 resolution. All student variants use 21-frame Evaluation. The 15s VBench evaluation uses Wan2.1-augmented prompts, with 5 videos generated per prompt. The 60s VBench-Long evaluation uses all 1,003 entries in the original MovieGenBench prompt list without prompt expansion. We generate 1 video per entry, with each rollout containing 1,005 frames. A.2 Out-of-sight World Modeling Training. Training camera trajectories use left/right rotations or translations followed by return to the initial viewpoint. The learning rate is 1 105, with LoRA rank 64, scaling parameter α = 128, and 0 dropout. No gradient accumulation is used, giving an effective batch size of 8. The EMA teacher is initialized from the student and updated after each optimization step with decay of 0.9999. For each training sample, we generate the student and fixed-view teacher rollouts online with shared initial noise and SDE transition noise. The fixed-view teacher rollout uses 12-frame KV window with 3 sink frames. Since the world model performs image-to-video generation, both inputs used for historical supervision retain 1 sink frame corresponding to the initial image. To reserve capacity for additional history within the models native attention window of 12 latent frames, the shared recent context is reduced to 4 student-generated latent frames. The history-conditioned input additionally includes up to 4 earlier latent frames from the fixed-view teacher rollout. Inference. Evaluation uses the fine-tuned student weights. The student uses 12-frame KV window with 3 sink frames at 1280 704 resolution, generating 1 video per input. Evaluation. All models are evaluated using the same initial images, prompts, preset camera trajectories, and random seeds. Generation prompts describe the initial scene and its ongoing process, while task objectives are used only for evaluation. For the PlayWorld Out-of-sight subset [14], VLM-based scoring uses Doubao Seed 2.0 Lite. Raw Mean averages ratings before instruction gating, and Gated Mean assigns 16 score of 1 to videos that fail the instruction check. Evolution Quality measures the extent and causal plausibility of state evolution. Subject Identity measures subject and appearance consistency across revisits. Both metrics report mean 15 ratings before instruction gating. For the MemoBench Real subset [9], automated metrics are computed using the official MemoBench implementation.

sections.title: B Additional Qualitative Analysis
sections.content: Out-of-sight world modeling. Fig. 6 shows improved object preservation and scene evolution upon revisit. In the sand-filling example, the baseline accumulates sand outside the jar, while History Forcing keeps the sand predominantly inside it. History Forcing retains the tomatoes in the bowl, preserves the drinking glass as the coffee level rises, and keeps the purple solution inside the beaker. Some appearance and scene drift nevertheless remains. The fixed-camera teacher rollouts used for historical supervision can themselves contain temporal errors and exhibit limited scene evolution, as discussed in Section 6. These limitations reduce the accuracy of historical supervision and can contribute to inconsistencies upon revisit. 15-second video generation. Fig. 7 compares the DMD baseline and History Forcing on six 15s examples: violin performance in candle-lit chapel, desert carnival, bread baking, walk through Tokyo street, glacial cave, and Hong Kong tram. In the chapel example (a), the baseline background changes abruptly from the chapel interior to outdoor greenery between the displayed frames at 5.44s and 5.5s. In the carnival example (b), the baseline also changes the subjects appearance across frames. Across these examples, History Forcing better preserves the subjects, clothing, and surrounding scene at the sampled timestamps. 60-second video generation. Fig. 8 compares History Forcing with Self-Forcing, LongLive, and Rolling Forcing on 60s toothbrushing example. Self-Forcing develops severe color saturation and high-contrast artifacts as the rollout progresses. LongLive produces inconsistent toothbrush geometry, with the brush appearing as an elongated object grasped at both ends in several frames. Rolling Forcing distorts the mirror geometry: the reflected face extends beyond the mirror boundary, and the rim intersects the mouth and cheek. History Forcing maintains natural colors and more consistent toothbrush appearance and mirror geometry through 60s. Fig. 9 further shows that History Forcing maintains consistent clothing, object appearance, and scene layout across the 60s rollouts. 17 Figure 6 Additional qualitative comparisons of out-of-sight world modeling with the baseline and History Forcing: (a) sand filling, (b) tomatoes into bowl, (c) coffee pouring, and (d) purple solution pouring. 18 Figure 7 Additional qualitative comparisons of 15s video generation: (a) violin performance in candle-lit chapel, (b) desert carnival, (c) bread baking, (d) Tokyo street, (e) glacial cave, and (f) Hong Kong tram. Figure 8 Additional qualitative comparisons of 60s video generation: brushing teeth in front of mirror. 20 Figure 9 Additional qualitative examples of 60s video generation with History Forcing: (a) making dumplings, (b) playing an acoustic guitar, and (c) chef preparing dish in kitchen.
